name: Laundry sanitiser and strip washing

lead: Some people use sanitising additives or long soaks to get persistent smell out of workout clothes so the kit stops carrying a stale odour.

Sanitisers are meant to kill microorganisms in the wash, while strip washing is a heavy soak and wash intended to remove built-up residue. Wikipedia says high temperatures kill microorganisms, though it flags that as uncited. Body odour is attributed to bacteria acting on skin secretions, which can transfer to fabric. No source reviewed tests these methods.

paras: Gym-goers add a sanitiser to the wash or soak clothes before a normal wash, then dry thoroughly. It is mostly used on synthetic sports kit that holds smell.
Heat and agitation can shrink or damage some fabrics, so care labels apply.

web.title: Ghent University polyester odour study - EurekAlert

chain: Sanitiser or strip wash on gym kit
angle.text: Gym-goers use laundry sanitisers and heavy strip washes to remove odour-producing bacteria and built-up residue from sports clothing, so kit stops carrying a stale smell. Results are described through popular anecdotes.

lead: Laundry sanitiser and strip washing are practices used to remove persistent odour from gym and sports clothing, so that a person smells clean when training, commuting or meeting others. Sanitisers are additives intended to kill microorganisms in the wash, while strip washing is a heavy soak and wash intended to remove built-up residue from fabric. Practitioners say clothes that still smell after ordinary washing come back fresh after such treatment.

The underlying problem is documented. Sweat itself is largely odourless; the smell comes from bacteria acting on skin secretions, and Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species are among those implicated in body odour.[1] A 2014 Ghent University study led by Chris Callewaert collected t-shirts from 26 people after an hour of intensive cycling and found polyester shirts smelled worse than cotton, because odour-producing bacteria, mainly micrococci, grow better on polyester.[2] Wikipedia's laundry article says high temperatures kill microorganisms, though it flags the claim as uncited, and that drying at 60 degrees Celsius or higher for thirty minutes kills many mites.[3]

paras: Odour-causing bacteria such as Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species act on sweat secretions.[1] In the Ghent study, micrococci were the main odour-producing bacteria found on clothing, staphylococci produced normal body odour, and corynebacteria were the main cause of armpit odour but did not grow on textiles.[2]

Practitioners seeking to remove the resulting smell from clothes use hotter washes, additives or extended soaks. The Ghent researchers suggested polyester's surface properties may explain why it holds odour; the release advised that wearing cotton reduces the problem somewhat.[2]

Wikipedia notes that washing is sometimes done warmer to boost chemical activity and stain removal, that cotton should be washed cooler to avoid shrinking, and that heat plus agitation can shrink wool.[3] Garment care labels therefore set limits on how hot a wash can be.
No studies found of sanitisers or strip washing for removing odour from clothing. Research on odour in worn shirts exists (see Background).[2]

lore.intro: Community accounts describe odour that survives ordinary washing in gym clothes, especially synthetics.

claims.claim: Sanitiser or strip washing removes odour that normal washing leaves.
